title: (SLOW English) Learn the difference between school-taught grammar and real-life grammar in English!
channel: Speak English with Bo's Slow English

lines.text: Hello everyone. Welcome to a new episode
of Bo's Slow English. Today, we're
diving into an interesting topic, the
difference between grammar taught in
school and how people actually speak in
real life. Sometimes, the rules we hear
in the classroom does not match up to
what you hear in everyday conversations.
Stick around to find out why and how you
can sound more natural when you're
speaking English. Please like this video
and subscribe to my channel. It helps me
to know that I'm helping you and that
makes me very happy. In school, we learn
grammar rules that are designed to help
us speak and write in a clear,
standardized way. For example, we learn
never split an infinitive. To quickly
run should be to run quickly. Always use
proper subject-verb agreement. He is
going, not he are going. Avoid ending
sentences with prepositions. Where are
you at? Should be Where are you? These
rules are really useful for formal
writing, exams, and structured
communication.
But real life spoken English, it's not
always that strict. In everyday
conversations, native speakers usually
bend or break the rules to sound more
natural. Spoken English is much more
relaxed. Here are some common ways
grammar is used differently in real
life. Going back to split infinitives,
instead of to run quickly, people might
say to quickly run. Why? It just feels
more natural in conversation. Going back
to subject-verb agreement, in casual
speech, people might say things like,
"There's a bunch of people here." Even
though it should be, "There are a bunch
of people here." Why? It's faster and
simpler. And finally, going back to
ending with prepositions, you'll often
hear, "Who are you talking to?" rather
than the more formal, "To whom are you
talking?" The formal version sounds too
stiff in conversations. Please don't
speak like that. It sounds way too
formal. Another big difference between
formal, school-taught grammar and
real-life speech is the use of
contractions and shortened words. For
example, instead of saying, "I'm going
to." we say, "I'm going to." Instead of
saying, "Let me help you." we say, "Let
me help you." Instead of do not, it's
don't. These contractions make
conversations quicker and smoother. And
this is how most people speak
day-to-day. Spoken English is all about
efficiency. We often drop unnecessary
words, especially in informal settings.
Here are some examples. Dropping that.
In school, you learn to say, "I think
that it's a good idea." But in real
life, people drop that and say, "I think
it's a good idea." Dropping is or are.
In fast speech, people sometimes drop
words like is or are. For example,
instead of hearing, "The car is over
there." you might hear, "The car's over
there." Or even, "Car's over there."
Conversational ellipses. In everyday
talk, you might drop full phrases. For
example, "Do you want to go to the
store?" becomes, want to go to the
store. Do you want to go for a run
becomes want to go run. These shortcuts
save time in quick exchanges. In formal
English, you're taught to avoid double
negatives like I didn't do nothing. In
school, you'd be correct to say I didn't
do anything. But in casual speech,
especially in some regional dialects,
double negatives are common and
understood just fine. For example, I
ain't got no money instead of I don't
have any money. Or she doesn't know
nothing about that instead of she
doesn't know anything about that. These
aren't technically correct, but they're
part of spoken English in some areas. In
school, we're taught to use full
sentences. For example, I'm going to the
store because I need to buy some
groceries. But in real life
conversations, people often use sentence
fragments because they get the point
across faster. For example, going to the
store, need groceries or too tired,
can't go out. These fragments aren't
technically correct in writing, but in
conversation, everyone knows exactly
what you mean. Even native speakers make
common grammar mistakes, especially in
informal settings. Some of these include
saying me and him went to the store. Why
is it important to know both
school-taught grammar and real-life
spoken grammar? Well, formal grammar is
essential for writing essays,
professional emails, and giving
presentations. It helps you communicate
clearly and accurately in formal
settings. But spoken grammar is equally
as important because it helps you to
sound more natural in everyday
conversation. If you're too formal in
casual settings, it can come off as
awkward. And if you're too casual in
formal settings, it can make you seem
unprofessional. Knowing when to use each
style is key. If you want to improve
your real-life spoken English, here are
some tips. One, listen to native
speakers. Whether it's in movies, TV
shows, or podcasts, pay attention to how
they break the rules of grammar in
conversation. Number two, practice with
friends. Have casual conversations where
you can focus on sounding natural
instead of perfect. Number three, mimic
natural speech patterns. If you hear
someone use contractions or drop words
in conversation, try it out yourself.
Number four, don't be afraid to make
mistakes. In real-life speech, nobody
expects you to be perfect. It's more
important to communicate clearly and
naturally. Okay, there you have it.
Here's our lesson on the importance of
knowing both grammar rules taught in
school and everyday informal casual
conversations in English. Hopefully,
this was helpful for you. I know that
this topic can be pretty tricky for
people who are learning new languages.
Personally, I'm trying to learn French
and I know there's a lot of things that
I say that are a little too formal, but
I'm not quite at the level yet where I
feel comfortable to sound like a native
speaker. So, I hope you can apply these
rules that I discussed today and bend
the rules, and good luck. Thank you for
watching. Bye.
